verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, upon Jeduthun, of Asaph, a psalm.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, in the manner of Jeduthun: a psalm of Asaph.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is a stage direction, not part of the lament. Nothing in it is spoken in the voice of the sufferer; it tells the temple singers whose tune and whose collection this belongs to. Asaph and Jeduthun were Levitical musicians (see their entries in the names list), so the psalm is given to the professional choirs and sung aloud in the sanctuary, not murmured in private. Play the title plainly and let the grief begin after it.

The KJV numbers this title as verse 0 of its chapter, so every verse of the psalm sits one number lower in the KJV than in the Hebrew. It also reads the title as 'to Jeduthun', as if he were the addressee. The Hebrew preposition is 'al, 'upon', and the old commentators split on it: 'to', 'in the manner of', 'concerning' (Rashi on Psalm 77:1, Metzudat David), or a tune called Jeduthun (Ibn Ezra). The psalm itself says nothing to settle it.

philological_notes.note: Participle of the root meaning to be preeminent or to oversee, so a choirmaster or overseer of the temple music. The traditional 'chief Musician' is a fair reading, and the word heads dozens of psalm titles.

Read as 'for Jeduthun' by Radak and Meiri, who compare Hannah praying 'al YHWH (1 Sam 1:10) for 'to YHWH'. Rashi and Metzudat David take 'al as 'concerning' (the decrees that passed over Israel), and Ibn Ezra takes Jeduthun as the name of a tune.

verses.translation_literal: My voice [is] to God, and I will cry out; my voice [is] to God, and he will give ear to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: My voice goes to God, and I cry out. My voice goes to God, and let him bend his ear to me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The opening has no verb in its first clause: 'my voice to God'. It is a cry before it is a sentence. The speaker repeats the whole phrase, and the repetition is the acting note: the second 'my voice to God' is not decoration but a person saying it again because the first time did not feel heard. Radak reads the doubling as emphasis: my voice is for you alone, so give ear to me.

The KJV makes both halves into tidy past narration, 'I cried... and he gave ear', which turns an ongoing plea into a report of a rescue already granted. The Hebrew verbs are imperfect and the last one is a form the commentators argue about (Ibn Ezra lists three readings of 'and he will give ear'). It can be a wish, a confident expectation, or a plain statement. Keep it open; the rest of the psalm shows that the answer has not come. Here, 'Elohim is the general word for God. The personal name is held back until verse 12.

philological_notes.note: A perfect-form verb with 'and', literally 'and he has given ear / will give ear'. Ibn Ezra records that some call it an irregular past, Moses says it is an imperative, and Ibn Ezra himself reads it as a verbal noun. The sense hovers between wish and expectation.

verses.translation_literal: In [the] day of my distress, the Lord I sought; my hand, [by] night, was poured out and did not grow numb; my soul refused to be comforted.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the day of my trouble I went looking for the Lord. And all night my hand ran on, spilled out, and would not go slack. My soul would take no comfort.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse has three beats, and each answers the one before. By day the speaker acts: he seeks the Lord. By night something else takes over: the hand. Last, the self refuses. The final clause is the cruelest, because the refusal is the speaker's own. Play it as someone who wants to be comforted and cannot permit it.

The middle phrase is the hard one and the English versions fall into two camps. The KJV says 'my sore ran in the night', following Rashi, who reads 'hand' as 'wound' (the hand being where a blow lands) and the verb as a wound that keeps oozing. The ASV and YLT say 'my hand was stretched out', as in outstretched prayer. The verb nigerah is Niphal of a root meaning to flow or be poured out, as water poured on the ground. Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Malbim take it as the hand, or the speaker's strength, melting and running away like water, from the same family of images as 'my roarings are poured out like water' (Job 3:24). I would not choose a single picture on stage; a hand that is spilled out, open, emptied, and still not allowed to rest suits all three.

The KJV's 'trouble' for tsarah is soft: it is a narrowing, a tight place. And its past-tense 'I sought' fits better here than in verse 2, since daytime seeking is a completed fact the night then undoes.

philological_notes.note: Niphal of the root meaning to flow or pour out. Metzudat Zion compares 'and it poured out' (Ps 75:9, 'ויגר מזה'). STEPBible's 'stretched out' follows a different reading of the same consonants; the flow reading matches the verb that follows.

'My hand'. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David take it as 'my wound' (the hand takes the blow); Ibn Ezra rejects an eye-socket reading attributed to an earlier scholar, and offers 'my strength' or 'my place'. Malbim takes it as a literal, oozing sore used as an image.
To grow numb, slack or cold. Radak and Metzudat Zion gloss it as slackening or weakening and compare 'the law is slack' (Hab 1:4). Meiri adds the temperature sense: 'cooling'.

verses.translation_literal: Let me remember God, and I murmur; let me muse, and my spirit wraps itself [in faintness]. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: I remember God, and I moan. I turn it over in my mind, and my spirit folds in upon itself, faint. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the psalm's first turn, and it is a trap. The speaker does the right thing: he remembers God. The result is not comfort but a low, animal sound. Hamah is the word for the growl of a dog, the moan of a dove and the roar of a crowd. He does not complain about God; he groans at the thought of him. Then he tries again, with 'asichah, to muse aloud or tell it over, and the spirit gives way.

The KJV's 'I remembered God, and was troubled' is a calm report. The Hebrew has two cohortative verbs ('let me remember... let me muse') that put the speaker in the act of choosing memory and being struck down by it. The KJV's 'overwhelmed' for tit'attef is also from a root that means to cover or to wrap: the spirit pulls itself over itself, as Radak and Metzudat Zion put it, a person bent double, folded into himself. Ibn Ezra compares those 'faint from hunger' (Lam 2:19). Staging: let the actor fold when he says it.

Selah, the first of three in this psalm, is a pause of uncertain meaning. Mark it with silence, not with a gesture.

philological_notes.note: Cohortative of a root for a low, inarticulate sound: moan, murmur, growl, roar. The final -yah is a spelling variant of the cohortative ending, as Ibn Ezra and Radak note.
Hithpael of a root for wrapping or covering, and so to grow faint, to droop. Radak and Metzudat Zion picture the person bent over, wrapped in themselves.

token_glosses.gloss: and it wraps itself in a faint

verses.translation_literal: You have seized the watches of my eyes; I am struck, and I do not speak.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have taken hold of my eyelids and will not let them close. The night wears on, and I lie awake in it, stricken, and no word will come.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first half is a knot of readings, and the actor must choose one. Radak takes שמורות as the night 'watches' (אשמרות): the speaker's eyes are held in a permanent vigil, brooding over his troubles till morning leaves him too broken to speak. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take the word as the eyelids themselves, the guards of the eye: God has gripped them so that they cannot shut, as a sleeper's would. Rashi, Malbim and Meiri's second reading turn it the other way: the eyes are held shut, glued in the stupor of a heart gone numb, and for Malbim the collapse of a dying man who can no longer see or speak. The dramatic layer chooses the sleepless vigil, the reading that fits the night of vv. 3-7; play it as one choice among three.

The KJV's 'holdest mine eyes waking' follows the vigil reading and is sound, but it smooths over the grammar: the Hebrew has God as the grasping subject, and the verb אחז is the physical 'seize', used of a hand gripping. 'I am so troubled that I cannot speak' invents a cause ('so... that'); the Hebrew simply sets two short clauses side by side, with no connective but 'and'. The verb נפעמתי is a striking, a being beaten or jolted, as Pharaoh's spirit is 'troubled' in Gen 41:8 (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion), the same root as the word for a clapper-bell (פעמון), so the speaker rings with shock and is silenced. Silence here follows the moaning of v. 4 and the sealed lips of a man with nothing left to say.

philological_notes.note: From the root 'to guard, watch'. Read as the night watches (אשמרות), as the eyelids that guard the eye, or as the guarded, held-shut eyes; the commentaries split three ways.
A passive of the root 'to strike', as in the spirit 'troubled' in Gen 41:8; the idea is a blow that shakes the speaker into silence. Metzudat Zion links it to פעמון, the clapper-bell.

verses.translation_literal: I have reckoned days from of old, years of ages.
verses.translation_dramatic: I count back through the days of long ago, the years of ages past.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker reaches for the past. After a sleepless night and a spirit folded in on itself, the mind does arithmetic: chashavti is the word for reckoning, counting and weighing, as a merchant tallies accounts. He is not reminiscing; he is trying to total something up, to find where the balance went wrong. Ibn Ezra stresses the sense of 'accounting and dividing matters in the mind'.

The second line says the same thing again in other words, 'years of ages' for 'days from of old', as Radak says (the matter is doubled with different words). So the voice should widen, not move forward. The KJV's 'considered' makes it sound calm and scholarly, and 'ancient times' flattens 'olamim, a plural of the word for the farthest horizon of time. 'Days' and 'years' together mark the scale shift: from an ordinary night to the whole of history.

The commentators already hear the exile in it, Rashi the kindnesses done to our fathers, but the verse itself names no event. Do not supply one.

philological_notes.note: A root of reckoning and planning. Ibn Ezra ties it to counting and dividing in the mind. Used of thought that is deliberate, not drifting.
'Years of ages', the plural of 'olam. Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as a restatement of 'days of old', long spans of time.

verses.translation_literal: Let me remember my song in the night; with my heart let me muse, and my spirit searches.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the night I call back my song. I speak with my own heart, and my spirit goes searching.
verses.directors_commentary:
Neginah is a song with strings, a stringed melody, from the same root as the verb for playing. The speaker is, by the title, one of the temple musicians, and what he remembers is a song he used to play. Rashi hears the Temple, Radak the time after Egypt. The night this time is not the night of insomnia from verse 5 but the night in which he hears his own music in memory. It is the warmest line so far, and also the sharpest: the memory of a song is no consolation.

The actor can hum, or very quietly play a single phrase. Then the verse does what the earlier ones did: 'I muse' ('asichah) returns from verse 4 and the spirit, which folded in verse 4, now moves. 'And my spirit searches' is a different tense: a plain narrative form, not a wish. The KJV's 'made diligent search' translates it as past and adds 'diligent'. The Hebrew verb chafas is the verb for combing through something, as a house is searched, so the spirit is going through its rooms. Ibn Ezra points out that the object, 'me' or 'the matter', is missing, and the verb simply hangs, which keeps the question wide open as verse 8 begins.

The KJV's 'commune with mine own heart' is lovely but archaic: the Hebrew is 'with my heart', where the heart, in Hebrew, is the mind.

philological_notes.note: A song sung or played to strings, from the root meaning to play a stringed instrument. Rashi takes it as the songs once played in the Temple; Meiri as prayer or a prophecy of rescue.
To search thoroughly, to comb through. Metzudat Zion glosses it as investigation. Ibn Ezra notes the object is left unsaid.

verses.translation_literal: Will my Lord reject for the ages, and not add to show favor again?
verses.translation_dramatic: Will the Lord throw us off for ages? Will he never again add his favor?
verses.directors_commentary:
The question that the whole psalm has been circling finally gets said out loud. It comes as a string of five questions (verses 8 to 10), and this is the first. It begins with the little question particle he-, stuck to the front of the word 'for the ages' so the very first syllable is a question. The 'ol of 'olam, the word the speaker used for the past in verse 6, now points forward: he counted the ages behind him, now he fears the ages ahead.

Yizna'ch is a strong verb: to reject, to cast off, to discard something that no longer serves, used elsewhere of a nation or a sanctuary abandoned. The KJV's 'cast off' is right, and it is the one place the old English holds. But 'will he be favourable no more' loses the Hebrew idiom 'will he add to show favor': yosif is 'to add', the verb for doing something further. The speaker is asking whether there is an 'again' left, whether the account has a next line. Note that the plural of the question works against its own answer: Malbim hears each question in these verses as a rhetorical 'no', and the Targum asks 'is it possible?'. As a director, do not let the actor hear the 'no'. The speaker does not know it yet.

Adonai, 'my Lord', here is the title the speaker has used since verse 3, deliberately not the covenant name.

philological_notes.note: To reject, spurn, cast off. Metzudat Zion glosses it as abandonment ('azivah). It is the verb a people fears when it thinks it has been given up.
Literally 'will he not add to be pleased': the idiom for 'will he do so no more'. Radak reads it as 'as he used to favor Israel in times past'.

verses.translation_literal: Has his loyal love ceased for ever? Has [his] word come to an end for generation and generation?
verses.translation_dramatic: Is his faithful love gone for good? Has his word run out, for every generation after generation?
verses.directors_commentary:
The second question lifts the stakes from a mood to a promise. Chesed is the word for covenant loyalty, the steady, bound-by-oath love that God is said to keep (it is in the thirteen attributes of Exod 34:6). To ask whether it has 'ceased' is to ask whether the agreement itself has lapsed. The word the KJV renders 'mercy' is too soft; 'mercy' suggests mood, and chesed is obligation.

The second half is the more daring. 'Omer is 'a word, a saying'. The KJV's 'promise' is a good reading, and Rashi hears a decree: has he decreed forever that he will not relent? Ibn Ezra offers two glosses of gamar 'omer, 'a word is finished' and 'he has decreed a word that he will forever reject me'. Radak reads it as the words of comfort having run out. Either way it is a promise addressed to each generation, 'from generation to generation', and the speaker is asking whether the stream stops with his.

The verb 'afes is the verb of 'there is no more': as a purse is emptied (Gen 47:15, 'the money is gone', cited by Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion). The speaker is counting what remains and finding nothing. Say it as an auditor, not a rhetorician.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, loving-kindness that rests on a bond. The KJV's 'mercy' loses the sense of obligation.

Literally 'a word has come to an end / been finished'. Rashi takes it as 'a decree of eternity', Ibn Ezra as 'he decreed a saying that he will always cast me off', Radak and Metzudat David as 'the words of comfort have run out'. The Hebrew allows both 'come to an end' and 'decided'.

token_glosses.gloss: has it come to an end

verses.translation_literal: Has God forgotten to be gracious, or has he shut up in anger his compassions? Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Has God forgotten how to be kind? Or has his anger clenched shut his compassion? Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The third question is the sharpest, because it offers God two accusations and lets the speaker not choose. Either God forgot (a failing of memory) or he is angry (a failing of temper). The speaker, who has been remembering for nine verses, accuses God of the very thing he has been doing: forgetting. The irony is for the actor to find.

The verb qafatz is to shut, to draw closed: of a hand (Deut 15:7, 'do not shut your hand' to a poor brother, cited by both Rashi and Metzudat Zion) and of a mouth. So the picture is a fist closing. The KJV's 'shut up' is right, but the 'tender mercies' it puts after is a famous Elizabethan phrase that hides the Hebrew. Rachamim is the plural of rechem, the womb: it is compassion with a mother's body behind it. God's compassions are 'wombs', and they are what he has clenched shut. This is the strongest image in the psalm, and the KJV buries it.

Channoth 'El, 'to be gracious', is an infinitive that Rashi compares to 'asot and re'ot (Gen 2:4, Exod 10:28). Chanan is gracious favor given freely, as against chesed, which is owed. So the speaker has now asked about the bond (verse 9) and about the gift (verse 10). Selah closes the run of questions. Leave a long silence.

philological_notes.note: Plural of the noun for womb (rechem), hence compassion in the strongest sense, the feeling of a mother. Traditional 'tender mercies' keeps only half of this.
To close, draw together, as a hand held shut; Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion cite 'do not shut your hand' (Deut 15:7).
Infinitive of the root for showing grace. Rashi compares its form to 'asot and re'ot, and offers 'acts of grace' (chaninot) as another reading.

verses.translation_literal: And I said: my sickness, it, years of the right hand of the Most High.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I said: this is my wound, my sickness, this: the years, the changed years, of the right hand of the Most High.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is one of the hardest lines in the Psalter, and a director should say so to the actors. The Hebrew is a verbless sketch with four doubtful pieces, and the commentators produce at least three different sentences from it.

The first doubt is challoti. Rashi and Metzudat David take it from the root 'be sick': 'my sickness'. Radak and Meiri take it from the root for 'pierced, slain': 'my dying', so the speaker says that exile will be his grave. Metzudat Zion hears 'trembling'. The second doubt is shenot: 'years' (as in verse 6, 'years of ages'), or 'changes', from the root shanah, 'to alter' (Rashi, Metzudat David, Targum). On the second reading the speaker says: my sickness is this, that the right hand of the Most High has changed. On the first, the speaker says: my sickness is the years of the right hand. In both versions, the right hand is God's power, the one that fought for Israel.

The KJV smooths all of this by adding words the Hebrew does not have: 'This is my infirmity: but I will remember'. The 'but I will remember' is imported from the next verse (Radak and Meiri allow it, reading the next verse's 'I will remember' backward to cover this one). That turns a collapse into a recovery. The Hebrew has no such turn yet. Stage it as the lowest point: 'And I said', quietly, to himself.

The verse is also the first mention of the Most High, 'Elyon, the title that places God above every other power.

philological_notes.note: Disputed. From חלה 'be sick' (my sickness: Rashi, Metzudat David); from חלל 'pierce, die' (my dying: Radak, Meiri); from חיל 'tremble' (Metzudat Zion). Ibn Ezra lists a further reading from 'to entreat'.
Either 'years' (from shanah, as in verse 6) or 'changes' (from the root 'to alter'). Rashi, Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion and the Targum read 'change'; Meiri and Radak read 'years'.

The right hand of the Most High, the arm of battle and rescue. Rashi cites Exod 15:6, 'Your right hand, YHWH, is majestic in power, your right hand shatters the enemy', and Lam 2:3, 'he drew back his right hand'.

verses.translation_literal: I will remember the deeds of Yah, for I will remember from of old your wonder.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will remember the deeds of Yah. Yes: I will remember your wonders from long ago.
verses.directors_commentary:
Something turns here, and it turns in the grammar before the mood. The speaker has asked questions for four verses and now makes two statements, and the second begins 'for': a reason. He does not say the pain is over; he says what he will do with it. Remembering, which in verse 4 only made him moan, becomes a decision.

The name changes too. For the first time in the psalm the divine name appears, in its short form, Yah, the name that echoes inside 'hallelu-Yah'. Before this he has said 'Elohim, 'Adonai, 'El and 'Elyon. Now the covenant name arrives, and with it the grammar swings from talking about God ('the deeds of Yah') to speaking to him ('your wonder'). The KJV's 'the works of the LORD' puts the full name where the Hebrew has the short one and hides the shift in person. The KJV also adds 'surely' for ki; ki here is a plain 'for' or 'because'.

The written text (Ketiv) has 'ezkir, 'I will mention, I will cause to be remembered', and the reading tradition (Qere) 'ezkor, 'I will remember'. Radak notes both: first 'I will tell others', then 'I will remember, and be comforted'. The word 'deeds', ma'alalei, is a rare, weighty word for what someone has done, often with a trace of consequence; pele', 'wonder', is the word for the acts of God that cannot be explained, and it is singular here: one wonder, all of them, from before.

philological_notes.note: Reading (Qere): 'I will remember'. The written form (Ketiv) is 'ezkir, 'I will mention / cause to be remembered'. Radak explains both: tell others, and remember oneself.

'The deeds of Yah'. Ma'alal is an act with weight or consequence. Yah is the short form of the divine name, the one heard in 'hallelujah'. Malbim divides God's deeds into those that follow the order of nature and those that break it.
'Your wonder': an act beyond human explanation. The singular is collective. Radak ties it to the wonders at the Exodus; the text does not name them.

verses.translation_literal: And I will murmur over all your work, and on your deeds I will muse.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will turn over in my mind all that you have done, and of your deeds I will speak.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse answers v. 12 with two verbs of the inward voice: הגה and שיח. The first is the older, lower word, a murmur or mutter such as a man makes to himself when he reads or thinks aloud; the second is the plainer 'to muse, to talk over'. Between them the speaker moves from memory to speech. Metzudat Zion glosses והגיתי simply as 'thought' (ענין מחשבה) and אשיחה as 'speech and saying', and the dramatic layer follows that: the first clause is thought, the second is utterance. Radak adds why the singer does it: to comfort one's fellow with the great works at Egypt, the Reed Sea, Sinai and the wilderness, and Metzudat David says the memories are 'a restoring of the soul' to him.

The KJV's 'meditate also of... and talk of' is faithful in outline but blurs two things: the Hebrew repeats a pair of nearly synonymous words for work and doing (פעל, עלילה); Radak calls the second a doubling of the sense in other words. Radak notes that the first noun is written without its plural yod, so 'work' is a collective, 'all your doing'. For the actor: the word that opens the verse is quiet, almost under the breath, and the verse builds from it.

philological_notes.note: The root covers a low murmur or mutter (a growl, a dove's moan, a man reading to himself) and, by extension, to ponder; the lexical range is given in BDB. Metzudat Zion glosses this word as 'thought' (ענין מחשבה).
To muse, converse, speak over a matter; Metzudat Zion glosses it as speech and saying. It is the same verb as in v. 7, 'with my heart I speak', so the psalm closes the circle it opened.

verses.translation_literal: God, in the holy [is] your way. Who [is] a god great like God?
verses.translation_dramatic: O God, your way is holy ground: it runs through the sanctuary, set apart from every path we know. And who is there, among all that are called gods, who is great as God is great?
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker lifts his eyes from his own night to the whole sky of the gods. Read the first line slowly, almost as a whisper, and the question as a challenge thrown across a crowded room. In the ancient Near East every nation had its own gods and its own victories to boast of; this question is a claim that Israel's God is not one among them but the one against whom no comparison works.

The Hebrew 'baqodesh' is deliberately wide: 'in holiness' or 'in the holy place'. The KJV chooses 'in the sanctuary', which narrows it to the Temple, though ancient readers heard also 'in heaven' (Ibn Ezra, Meiri) or 'sanctity' (Rashi: your way is to sanctify your name by judging the wicked). The KJV also quietly adds 'our' in 'our God', which the Hebrew does not say. 'Elohim' as a name of God is also the word for 'gods', so the closing line sounds like a pun: who is a great god like God?

philological_notes.note: 'In holiness' or 'in the holy place'. Rashi explains the verse as God's way of sanctifying his name by judging the wicked; Meiri reads 'in heaven' by comparing Ps 89:7. The sense stays open.
'Like God' (or 'like the gods'): the same word is used for the one God and for gods in general, so the rhetorical question rests on the word itself.

verses.translation_literal: You [are] the God, doer of wonder. You made known among the peoples your strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: You are the God who works wonders. You did not hide your strength; you let the nations see it with their own eyes.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the speaker answers his own question with the name of the deed. 'You' stands first and alone: say it to God directly. In a world where kings proved their gods by conquest and made their victories known in inscriptions, the claim is that Israel's God did the same, but with wonders (pele), a word for what is beyond human doing, and in front of other peoples.

The KJV 'doest wonders' is fair, but 'thou hast declared thy strength' makes it sound like an announcement; the Hebrew hoda'ta is causative, 'you made known', as in 'you made them know'. The 'peoples' are not spectators in the story: Radak thinks of Egypt and the Canaanite kings, Meiri of the signs of the exodus. Ibn Ezra stresses that the wonders were hidden from ordinary human eyes but visible in their results.

philological_notes.note: 'Wonder', something too extraordinary for human power; it is used almost only of God's acts (Exod 15:11). Here the singular is collective: 'a doer of wonder'.
Hiphil: 'you caused to be known'. The audience is the nations, not only Israel, which is why the KJV 'declared' misses the causative sense.

verses.translation_literal: You redeemed, by an arm, your people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: With your own arm you bought them back, your people, the children of Jacob and of Joseph. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turning point of the psalm, the first named act in the remembered history: the Exodus, told in one verb. גאל is the kinsman's word. In Israelite law the go'el is the next of kin who buys back a relative's land or freedom (Lev 25), and BDB lists 'redeem' in this family sense; the word brings the idea that Israel is God's own flesh. Radak sharpens what the redeeming looked like: God redeemed his people not with the consent of their masters but by great compulsion and an outstretched arm. This was not a purchase at a fair price; the masters did not agree, and Pharaoh had to be overpowered. Metzudat David reads the Selah as the redemption complete forever, never again enslaved.

The arm is the image of power in action, and it takes up the 'right hand' of v. 11. Note too the odd pair at the end. 'The sons of Jacob and Joseph' is rare. Ibn Ezra and Radak explain Joseph as the one who fed the family through the famine, and so is father to them too (Metzudat David: Jacob begot them, Joseph sustained them); the KJV's 'the sons of Jacob and Joseph' keeps the words but not the reason, and nothing in the English tells the reader why the son stands next to his father as a father of the tribes. Joseph is also the name that opens the story of the whole descent into Egypt that this redemption reverses.

philological_notes.note: To redeem, to act as the kinsman (go'el) who recovers a relative from slavery or loss; the next-of-kin image is the lexical background (BDB). Radak stresses that God redeemed them by force, not with the masters' consent.
'By an arm': a strong arm, a figure of power; Radak glosses it with the full phrase 'an outstretched arm' (זרוע נטויה).
Why Joseph beside Jacob: he fed them through the famine and so is counted a father to them (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David).

verses.translation_literal: They saw you, waters, God; they saw you, waters; they writhed; also the deeps trembled.
verses.translation_dramatic: The waters saw you, O God. The waters saw you, and they writhed like something in labor. The very deeps, down in the dark, began to shudder.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poem now leaves the argument and enters the scene. The first line is a stutter of awe: 'they saw you, waters, God; they saw you, waters'. Let the repetition be the sound of a sea at the moment of seeing something it cannot bear. The waters are not a backdrop but a witness, and they react as living beings do in the Bible's picture of creation: the sea, which in neighbouring myth was a god who fought Baal or Marduk, here simply cowers when the real God appears. This is polemic by omission: no battle at all, only fear.

The verb yachilu is the verb for labor pains and for dancing in a circle (khul), so the waters 'writhe', as a woman in childbirth does, rather than the KJV's weak 'were afraid'. The same sense of a body in agony is lost in 'afraid'. The KJV also puts 'the depths also were troubled' where the Hebrew says the tehomot, the same deeps as in Gen 1:2, trembled: a pointed echo of creation in an exodus psalm. Rashi, Radak and Meiri tie all of it to the sea of Exodus 14.

philological_notes.note: To twist, writhe; used of childbirth pangs (Isa 26:17) and of trembling in fear. 'Were afraid' in KJV loses the bodily image. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'tremble'.
The deeps, the primeval waters of Gen 1:2; here they shudder like the sea. Radak and Metzudat David read them as the depth of the sea.

verses.translation_literal: They poured out [as] water, clouds; a sound they gave, skies; also your arrows went about.
verses.translation_dramatic: The clouds tore open and the water came down in torrents. The skies gave a voice, a long, low roar. And your arrows flew everywhere, back and forth across the dark.
verses.directors_commentary:
The storm breaks, and the camera moves upward. Notice that nothing here is in Exodus 14, which has no rain and no thunder; the psalm tells the crossing in the colours of a theophany, the way God appears on Sinai and in Canaanite poetry about the storm-god Baal-Hadad. That is the point. The god who rides the storm in Ugaritic poems was the rainmaker of the whole region, and the psalm gives his thunder and his lightning to the God of Israel.

The arrows are lightning: 'your arrows' (chatsatsekha) is a rare, ancient form, and Rashi and Metzudat David both read it as lightning, the arrows of God (as in Ps 18:15). Others, such as Meiri and Radak, hear small stones, hail or gravel, which fits the 'confusion' of the Egyptian camp in Exodus 14:24. The verb 'went about' (yit-halekhu) is a reflexive of walking: the arrows go back and forth, they pace. KJV 'went abroad' is archaic and unclear. The 'skies' (shechakim) are the thin high layers above the clouds, the dust of the heavens.

philological_notes.note: 'Your arrows', a poetic doubled form of khets. Rashi says it equals 'your arrows' and Metzudat David says it means lightning; Radak and Meiri propose 'gravel, stones', a rare alternative.
The skies, from a root meaning 'to rub fine' or 'to pulverize', the thin upper air; Metzudat Zion glosses 'firmaments'.

verses.translation_literal: [The] voice of your thunder [was] in the wheel; lightning flashes lit up [the] world; the earth trembled and shook.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then your thunder spoke, and it rolled, a great wheel turning over the deep. Lightning tore the dark open and lit the whole world white. The ground shuddered beneath it. The earth trembled, and went on shaking.
verses.directors_commentary:
Open with sound, not light: the voice of thunder comes first, and it is a rolling sound. The odd word is galgal, 'wheel'. The KJV smooths it into 'in the heaven', and the YLT has 'in the spheres'. That is the reading of Radak and Ibn Ezra, who take the wheel to be the turning sky or the rolling air. The ASV's 'whirlwind' is a guess from the same root, which means rolling. The commentators also read it more concretely. Rashi takes the word as 'like a wheel': the voice of your thunder like a wheel over the sea, a rumble that threw the camp of Egypt into confusion (he points to Exod 14:24). Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion and Meiri hear the wheels of Pharaoh's chariots, and Metzudat David cites Exod 14:25, 'he removed the wheel of their chariots'. Play the line so that the audience can hear both: a sound that rolls.

The verbs shake in pairs. 'Lit up' is the causative of 'or', 'light': the lightning makes the world bright, and the KJV's 'lightened the world' is a stiff old English echo of that. Then the earth 'trembled' and 'shook', two verbs of quaking, with the earth as a feminine subject that answers like a person overcome by fear. Radak ties the shaking to Egypt's own trembling and quaking. For an ancient audience, thunder, lightning and quake are the weapons of the storm god, as Baal was in Canaanite myth; here they belong to YHWH alone, who has no rival to ride them.

philological_notes.note: A wheel, from the root 'to roll'. Radak and Ibn Ezra read the sky or the air as the rolling sphere; Rashi reads the word as 'like a wheel' (kegalgal), thunder rolling over the sea; Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion and Meiri hear the wheels of Pharaoh's chariots, the first two as 'the wheel of a cart'. The word needs no emending to carry any of these.
The causative of 'to be light': the lightning flashes made the world bright. Radak compares 'and it lit up the night' (Exod 14:20).
The inhabited, fertile world, often in parallel with 'earth' as here; it adds the sense of everything that lives on the ground that shakes.

verses.translation_literal: In the sea [was] your way, and your path in many waters, and your footprints were not known.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your road ran through the sea, your path through the great waters, and no one saw where you had set your feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now turns to the most surprising thing of all. God's way is through the sea, the one place where no road can be kept: a path that only exists while it is walked on, and leaves no trace. The speaker, who began the psalm looking for a sign of God and finding none, now says that this silence was always the way God travels. Let the actors lower the voices: this is the verse of mystery, not of the display of power.

The KJV 'thy footsteps are not known' is correct but misses the sound: 'ikvotekha' is 'heels', so the word is literally 'your heel-prints', as a tracker would say. The sea closed behind God and Israel, so Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David all say the footprints could not be seen because the waters returned at once to their place. A tracker's eye is the right actor's eye: the text uses the language of hunters who read the ground. 'Many waters' in the KJV is 'great waters'; in Hebrew 'mayim rabbim' is an idiom for the deep and chaotic sea. Radak notices the Ketiv: the written form is the plural 'your paths', which he explains as the twelve paths of the tribes.

philological_notes.note: Read as singular 'your path' (Qere); the written text has the plural 'your paths'. Radak takes the plural to mean twelve paths, one for each tribe, from Ps 136:13.
'Your heel-prints', from 'heel' (aqev); Rashi glosses it as 'tracks' (a French word, terṣ”sh). A word for a tracker's mark on the ground.

verses.translation_literal: You led your people like the flock, by [the] hand of Moses and Aaron.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then the storm was gone, and the sea lay behind them. You led your people the way a shepherd leads his flock, quietly, step after step, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on its softest note. After the thunder, the verb is gentle: nachah, 'to lead', in the sense of guiding a flock and guarding it. Radak says this is how a shepherd leads his sheep and keeps them; Metzudat Zion glosses it simply 'you drove, you conducted'. Ibn Ezra offers two readings: the crossing of the sea, as beasts go down into a valley, or the later march through the wilderness. Radak chooses the wilderness, after the people came up out of the sea. Metzudat David adds that the speaker turns back to the beginning of the psalm: remembering all this, he knows that God did not fail to redeem for lack of power.

The KJV's 'leddest' is archaic but accurate. What it cannot show is the small word 'the' in 'like the flock': Hebrew says 'like the flock', as if everyone knew which one. The flock is a people, and the shepherd is God; Moses and Aaron are only his hand. 'By the hand of' is a standard way of saying 'through the agency of', and the order, Moses first, matches the order of their prophetic rank, as Ibn Ezra observes. Nothing of God's own footprints was visible in verse 20; here the visible leaders are named, and they are the only human actors in the psalm. Play them small.

philological_notes.note: To lead, guide. Radak: the way a shepherd leads and guards his flock; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'you drove, you conducted'.
'By the hand of': the two are the instrument of God's leading, not its source. Ibn Ezra notes that Moses comes before Aaron because of the greatness of his prophecy.
